1	\section{Experiments}\label{sec:experiments}
2	
3	\subsection{Experimental Setup}\label{sec:setup}
4	
5	\paragraph{Datasets.}
6	We evaluate on four English NER benchmarks spanning a difficulty gradient.
7	\textbf{SciERC} \cite{luan2018scierc} (551 test instances, 6 entity types) is the primary medium-difficulty test bed (${\approx}$65\% F1).
8	\textbf{Few-NERD} \cite{ding2021fewnerd} (INTRA coarse; 37{,}648 instances, 8 entity types, ${\approx}$75\% F1) provides a low-degeneracy contrast where LP selection succeeds (\S\ref{sec:selection_gap}).
9	\textbf{CoNLL-2003} \cite{tjongkimsang2003conll} (3{,}453 test sentences, 4 entity types, ${\approx}$91\% F1) serves as a ceiling-effect control.
10	\textbf{WNUT-17} \cite{derczynski2017wnut} (1{,}287 social media instances, 53.7\% zero F1) probes the signal-collapse boundary.
11	
12	\paragraph{Models and sampling.}
13	\textbf{Qwen3-8B} and \textbf{LLaMA-3.1-8B-Instruct} are LoRA fine-tuned using LLaMA Factory \cite{zheng2024llamafactory} (Appendix~\ref{app:training}; Few-NERD uses 3 epochs vs.\ 5 for others; Appendix~\ref{app:epoch_confound}).
14	$N{=}8$ samples at $T{=}1.0$ (primary) with vLLM constrained decoding \cite{willard2023guided}; $N {\in} \{16, 32, 64\}$ for scaling (Figure~\ref{fig:n_scaling}; Appendix~\ref{app:n_scaling}).
15	
16	\begin{figure}[t]
17	\centering
18	\includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{figures/fig_n_scaling_mv.pdf}
19	\caption{MV $\Delta$F1 vs.\ $\log_2 N$ across three datasets (Qwen3-8B FT, seed${=}42$). Dotted gray: $\Delta{=}0$. Gains are dataset-dependent: persistently negative on Few-NERD, near zero on SciERC at higher $N$, marginally positive on CoNLL ($+0.6$\,pp at $N{=}64$).}
20	\label{fig:n_scaling}
21	\end{figure}
22	
23	%% ============================================================
24	\subsection{Quality Estimation Results}\label{sec:qe_results}
25

27	\centering

30	\label{tab:quality_estimation}
31	\begin{tabular}{ll cc cc cc}
32	\toprule
33	& & \multicolumn{2}{c}{\textbf{SciERC}} & \multicolumn{2}{c}{\textbf{CoNLL (Qwen)}} & \multicolumn{2}{c}{\textbf{CoNLL (LLaMA)}} \\

35	Signal & Family & $\rho$ & AUC & $\rho$ & AUC & $\rho$ & AUC \\

46	
47	Table~\ref{tab:quality_estimation} presents $\rho$ and AUROC for five signals across tasks and models.
48	
49	\paragraph{Signal rankings are difficulty-dependent.}
50	On SciERC, structural signals lead (VC $\rho{=}0.379$, SJ $0.360$) over LP ($0.205$); bootstrap CIs confirm the gap ($\Delta\rho{=}{+}0.151{\pm}0.006$, 5 seeds; Appendix~\ref{app:bootstrap_signal}).
51	Under seed-replication Holm--Bonferroni correction ($k{=}5$ seeds), the SJ~${>}$~LP advantage reaches $p_{\text{adj}}{=}0.013$ (Appendix~\ref{app:bootstrap_signal}).
52	On CoNLL (F1${\approx}$0.91), EM leads both $\rho$ and AUROC ($0.816$).
53	At the signal-collapse boundary (WNUT-17, F1${\approx}$42\%), full-set correlations are dominated by the zero/non-zero boundary (VC $\rho{=}0.724$ at $N{=}16$, but conditional $\rho{=}0.038$; Table~\ref{tab:wnut}); LP shows the reverse (conditional $\rho{=}0.350$; Figure~\ref{fig:signal_heatmap}).

56	\subsection{Cross-Dataset Contrast: Few-NERD}\label{sec:fewnerd}
57	
58	\begin{table}[t]

60	\small

64	\begin{tabular}{@{}lrccccr@{}}
65	\toprule
66	Dataset & $n$ & Greedy & Degen.\% & LP $\rho$ & LP $\Delta$ & $p$ \\

Training convergence modulates degeneracy (5-epoch: $31$\%, LP $\Delta$ collapses from $+1.39$ to $+0.09$\,pp; Appendix~\ref{app:epoch_confound}).
77	
78	Signal ranking is task-specific; per-type analysis shows MV degradation concentrates in low-F1 types ($\rho{=}0.90$, $p{=}0.002$; Appendix~\ref{app:pertype}).
79	
80	\paragraph{Degeneracy alone does not predict LP direction.}
81	Degeneracy does not predict LP gain across 23 configurations ($\rho{=}0.052$, $p{=}0.81$; $n{=}23$, insufficient for reliable correlation---we treat this as supplementary evidence; Figure~\ref{fig:degeneracy_scatter}), though it co-varies with LP within fixed settings ($\rho{=}{-}0.881$; Appendix~\ref{app:per_type_lp}).

86	\caption{Instance degeneracy vs.\ LP selection gain across 23 configurations ($N{=}8$; $\rho{=}0.052$, $p{=}0.81$). Within Few-NERD per-entity-type ($\rho{=}{-}0.881$; Appendix~\ref{app:per_type_lp}), degeneracy predicts LP gain when alignment is held constant.}
87	\label{fig:degeneracy_scatter}
88	\end{figure}

90	MV gains range from $-2.71$\,pp (Few-NERD) to $+0.6$\,pp (CoNLL at $N{=}64$; Figure~\ref{fig:n_scaling}); the optimal strategy is dataset-dependent (LP-best $+1.4$\,pp on Few-NERD vs.\ MV $+0.61$\,pp on CoNLL).
91	The framework extends to RE, where $40$\% zero-F1 from upstream entity span errors creates a distinct failure mode---\textit{diversity among failures} rather than quality-differentiated outputs---despite comparable degeneracy ($10.1$\% vs.\ SciERC $13.4$\%; Appendix~\ref{app:re_extension}).
92	
93	%% ============================================================
94	\subsection{Robustness}\label{sec:robustness_main}
95	
96	Signal rankings are robust across temperatures, seeds, and $N$ (Table~\ref{tab:robustness}; Appendix~\ref{app:calibration}); Qwen3-4B QE matches 8B ($|\Delta\rho|{=}0.042$).
97	The gap persists from 4B to 72B zero-shot to GPT-5.5 (\S\ref{sec:scaling}).
98	
99	%% ============================================================
100	\subsection{Entity Construction (Exploratory)}\label{sec:prescriptive}
101	
102	Given that sample-level selection yields no detectable gains across configurations (\S\ref{sec:selection_gap}), we ask whether entity-level aggregation can extract value from multi-sample generation under favorable diagnostic conditions.
103	
104	\paragraph{Entity-level construction (exploratory).}
105	We aggregate entities across samples, retaining those exceeding $\theta{=}2/N$, with LP-weighted or uniform scoring ($\theta$ stable in $[0.15, 0.35]$; Appendix~\ref{app:theta_sweep}).
106	The diagnostic framework identifies conditions favoring gains: low degeneracy and strong LP alignment.
107	LP-weighted construction yields $+1.40{\pm}0.51$\,pp on Few-NERD (3-seed mean; $p{<}0.001$; Table~\ref{tab:entity_construction}), consistent with these conditions ($D{=}13$\%, headroom${=}12.4$\,pp), a smaller non-significant $+0.32$\,pp on SciERC, and no gain on CoNLL ($-0.39$\,pp).\footnote{Degenerate instances contribute $\Delta{=}0$ by construction; gains concentrate in the non-degenerate subset ($+3.36$\,pp SciERC, $+5.18$\,pp CoNLL, $+7.08$\,pp Few-NERD).}
108	We group the 57 comparisons into methodological families---per-sample signals ($k{=}21$), cross-sample signals ($k{=}26$), and entity construction ($k{=}10$)---reflecting mechanistic distinctions defined at experiment design time (not selected post-hoc to optimize $p$-values).
109	Under global Holm--Bonferroni \cite{holm1979simple} correction across all $k{=}57$ comparisons, $p_{\text{adj}}{=}0.055$ (suggestive); under per-family correction within the 10-comparison entity-construction family, $p_{\text{adj}}{=}0.006$ (significant); BH FDR: $6/10$ construction comparisons at FDR${<}0.05$ (Appendix~\ref{app:holm}).
110	We report all three corrections for transparency; the family partition was not pre-registered.
111	Construction and LP selection are complementary ($\rho_{\text{adj}}$: Few-NERD $0.516$); QE signals support selective prediction ($+5$--$8$\,pp at 80\% coverage; Table~\ref{tab:cross_selection}). Practitioners can compute $D$ and $\alpha$ on a pilot sample ($N{=}8$) to assess scaling viability before committing to repeated inference.
112	
113	\paragraph{Training convergence modulates scaling returns.}
114	Training convergence state is itself associated with SC efficacy: 5-epoch training on Few-NERD eliminates LP gains entirely (LP selection: $+1.39{\to}+0.12{\pm}0.04$\,pp, 91\% reduction, 2-seed mean; entity construction: $+0.88{\to}+0.20$\,pp, 77\% reduction, seed 42; Appendix~\ref{app:epoch_confound}).
115	The diagnostic framework is consistent with this observation: 5-epoch constant-F1 degeneracy rises to $31$\% (vs.\ $13$\% at 3 epochs), degrading conditions for both selection and construction.\footnote{Degeneracy rates vary by definition: constant-F1 degeneracy (all $N$ samples yield identical F1) gives $31$\%/$13$\%; entity-set exact-match degeneracy gives $26$\%/$9$\%. The directional pattern is consistent.}
116	This suggests SC may complement early stopping strategies---under-converged models preserve output diversity that enables aggregation gains, while fully converged models exhibit degeneracy that renders scaling ineffective (note: 3-epoch greedy F1 $0.748$ vs.\ 5-epoch $0.798$; part of the larger $\Delta$ may reflect greater headroom under a weaker baseline).
117	
118	\phantomsection\label{sec:selection_results}
119

1	\begin{abstract}
2	Test-time compute scaling---repeated sampling with self-consistency or best-of-$N$---yields large gains on discrete-answer reasoning, but whether these gains transfer to NER remains open.
3	We characterize when scaling succeeds and fails, using NER (four datasets, primarily 7--14B fine-tuned) as the primary analysis, with preliminary cross-task pilots (RE, SQL).
4	Quality estimation signals predict output quality (AUROC up to $0.82$), yet instance-level selection yields no detectable gains (${<}1$\,pp; CI crosses zero), revealing a \textbf{correlation-selection gap}.
5	A diagnostic framework identifies two co-occurring conditions---\textit{degeneracy} (i.e., multiple outputs collapsing to identical predictions) and signal alignment collapse---that are jointly associated with scaling returns; cross-task exploration confirms task-specific failure modes.
6	Entity-level construction yields conditional gains ($+1.40$\,pp on Few-NERD under 3-epoch training; collapses at convergence; global Holm $p_{\text{adj}}{=}0.055$, suggestive; per-family $p_{\text{adj}}{=}0.006$, post-hoc family partition) but exhibits inverse scaling in most configurations.
7	The framework is primarily diagnostic, with limited predictive power for identifying favorable conditions, informing resource allocation decisions before investing in repeated inference.
8	\end{abstract}
9

\begin{abstract}
Test-time compute scaling---repeated sampling with self-consistency or best-of-$N$---yields large gains on discrete-answer reasoning, but whether these gains transfer to NER remains open.
We characterize when scaling succeeds and fails, using NER (four datasets, primarily 7--14B fine-tuned) as the primary analysis, with preliminary cross-task pilots (RE, SQL).
Quality estimation signals predict output quality (AUROC up to $0.82$), yet instance-level selection yields no detectable gains (${<}1$\,pp; CI crosses zero), revealing a \textbf{correlation-selection gap}.
A diagnostic framework identifies two co-occurring conditions---\textit{degeneracy} (i.e., multiple outputs collapsing to identical predictions) and signal alignment collapse---that are jointly associated with scaling returns; cross-task exploration confirms task-specific failure modes.
Entity-level construction yields conditional gains ($+1.40$\,pp on Few-NERD under 3-epoch training; collapses at convergence; global Holm $p_{\text{adj}}{=}0.055$, suggestive; per-family $p_{\text{adj}}{=}0.006$, post-hoc family partition) but exhibits inverse scaling in most configurations.
The framework is primarily diagnostic, with limited predictive power for identifying favorable conditions, informing resource allocation decisions before investing in repeated inference.
\end{abstract}

1	\section{Threshold Regime Analysis}\label{sec:theory_scaling}
2	
3	\subsection{Entity Construction as MBR Decoding}\label{sec:mbr_theory}
4	
5	Entity-level construction selects $\hat{y}_{\textup{MBR}} = \{e \in E_\cup : \hat{p}(e) > \alpha/(\alpha{+}1)\}$ under balanced set-overlap utility; $\alpha{=}1$ recovers majority vote (Proposition~\ref{prop:construction_mbr}; Table~\ref{tab:entity_construction}; Appendix~\ref{app:mbr_proof}).
6	Signal-derived weights $w_i$ yield quality-weighted MBR: $\hat{p}_w(e) = \sum_{i} w_i \, \mathbf{1}[e {\in} y_i] / \sum_{i} w_i$; weighting improves when $w_i$ correlates with instance quality but degrades otherwise (LP on SciERC: $\rho{\approx}0.2$; \S\ref{sec:prescriptive}), consistent with utility degradation on structured outputs \cite{eikema2025structured}.
7	We select $\varepsilon{=}0.05$ at the elbow of the compression curve, where LP-best selection advantage transitions from $+1.5$\,pp (compressed) to $+4.6$\,pp (non-compressed; Appendix~\ref{app:fewnerd_epsilon}).
8	
9	\subsection{Scaling and Inverse Scaling}\label{sec:scaling}
10	
11	Oracle F1 follows $F_1(N) = a - b \cdot N^{-c}$ ($R^2 > 0.999$; Figure~\ref{fig:oracle_scaling}): Few-NERD ($c{\approx}0.61$) scales comparably to reasoning tasks \cite{brown2024monkeys}, SciERC converges more slowly ($c{\approx}0.35$), yet confidence-based aggregation recovers ${<}1$\,pp---a persistent gap.
12	The gap persists across scales and families: scaling from 8B to 14B FT increases oracle headroom ($+1.2$\,pp) with minimal greedy gain ($+0.9$\,pp), and GPT-5.5 (200 Few-NERD instances, zero-shot) exhibits the same pattern---50\% degeneracy, SJ $\rho{=}0.346$, MV $+1.4$\,pp yet 6.8\,pp oracle headroom unrealized.\footnote{Of the 10.1\% of GPT-5.5 samples producing empty entity sets, 88\% correspond to gold-empty instances; true parse failures affect only 1.2\% of samples (19/1{,}600) and shift all reported metrics by ${<}0.5$\,pp. See Appendix~\ref{app:frontier_sc}.}
13	Degeneracy is model-family-dependent rather than scale-dependent (Qwen2.5: $31.7$--$46.2$\% vs.\ Qwen3: $13.0$\% vs.\ GPT-5.5: $50$\% on Few-NERD; Appendix~\ref{app:cross_scale}).
14	
15	\paragraph{Inverse scaling under adaptive thresholds.}
16	Increasing $N$ \textit{decreases} construction F1 in 40 of 58 transitions ($p{<}0.05$; Appendix~\ref{app:n_scaling}).
17	Methods using $\theta{=}2/N$ are most affected ($-3.09$\,pp at $N{=}8$, $-6.90$\,pp at $N{=}16$ vs.\ greedy on Few-NERD); majority vote ($\theta{=}\tfrac{1}{2}$) reduces the delta to $-0.87$/$-0.60$\,pp---severity reduction, not immunity (Table~\ref{tab:theta_sweep}).
18	Inverse scaling concentrates in non-degenerate instances ($11.1$\% vs.\ $1.3$\% for degenerate; OR${=}0.109$; Appendix~\ref{app:degen_inverse}).
19	Few-shot demonstrations improve QE (CoNLL SJ $\rho$ $.30{\to}.44$) but not construction (all n.s.; Appendix~\ref{app:fs_error}).
20	
21	\subsection{Degeneracy Decomposition}\label{sec:theory}
22	
23	\noindent\textbf{Degeneracy Decomposition.}\label{thm:degeneracy_bound}
24	For any aggregation method $A$: $\mathbb{E}[\Delta F_1(A)] \leq (1 - D) \cdot G_{\textup{nd}}$,
25	where $D$ is the degeneracy rate and $G_{\textup{nd}}$ the oracle gap on non-degenerate instances.
26	For signal-based methods with alignment $\alpha \in [0,1]$, this tightens to $(1{-}D) \cdot G_{\textup{nd}} \cdot \alpha$ (proof in Appendix~\ref{app:bound_proof}).
27	
28	\noindent The bound is an intentionally loose \textit{necessary condition test}: when $D{\to}1$ or $\alpha{\to}0$, no aggregation method can improve over greedy, regardless of implementation.
29	It identifies \textit{where} aggregation fails---screening for favorable conditions---rather than quantitatively predicting gains.
30	Across 16 configurations, all gains respect the bound; the low recovery ratio (3--12\%; Figure~\ref{fig:bound}) reflects its role as a screening test, not a tight estimate.
31	$\alpha$---not $D$---is the binding constraint ($\alpha{=}0.000$--$0.161$; $8$--$33{\times}$ tighter), and this conclusion is robust to signal combination (\S\ref{sec:robustness_main}), verifier-based construction (\S\ref{sec:verifier}), and $\theta_{\text{crit}} \in [0.60, 0.80]$.
32	
33	\paragraph{Bound looseness.}
34	The decomposition is a necessary condition screen showing how degeneracy and alignment jointly suppress gains, not a quantitative prediction tool. Two sources of looseness dominate: (1)~the entity independence assumption---split-half correlation $r{=}0.578$--$0.644$ reveals substantial inter-entity correlation structure within instances, which the bound ignores; (2)~$\alpha$ is estimated conservatively as the minimum across instances rather than an instance-adaptive value, further widening the gap. Together these explain the 3--12\% recovery ratio (bound ratio $0.13$--$0.63$). The decomposition nonetheless identifies $\alpha{\to}0$, not degeneracy, as the binding constraint across all tested configurations.
35	
36	MV improves F1 only if marginal-entity precision exceeds $F_1^{\textup{gr}}/2$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:entity_selection_bound}; Appendix~\ref{app:alpha_crit}).
37	Table~\ref{tab:alpha_crit} validates: at $N{=}8$, no dataset meets this condition ($\Delta$ from $-2.74$ to ${\approx}0$\,pp); CoNLL ($\alpha_{\textup{crit,eff}}{=}1.148 {>} 1$) makes MV gain structurally impossible.
38

\section{Threshold Regime Analysis}\label{sec:theory_scaling}

\subsection{Entity Construction as MBR Decoding}\label{sec:mbr_theory}

Entity-level construction selects $\hat{y}_{\textup{MBR}} = \{e \in E_\cup : \hat{p}(e) > \alpha/(\alpha{+}1)\}$ under balanced set-overlap utility; $\alpha{=}1$ recovers majority vote (Proposition~\ref{prop:construction_mbr}; Table~\ref{tab:entity_construction}; Appendix~\ref{app:mbr_proof}).
Signal-derived weights $w_i$ yield quality-weighted MBR: $\hat{p}_w(e) = \sum_{i} w_i \, \mathbf{1}[e {\in} y_i] / \sum_{i} w_i$; weighting improves when $w_i$ correlates with instance quality but degrades otherwise (LP on SciERC: $\rho{\approx}0.2$; \S\ref{sec:prescriptive}), consistent with utility degradation on structured outputs \cite{eikema2025structured}.
We select $\varepsilon{=}0.05$ at the elbow of the compression curve, where LP-best selection advantage transitions from $+1.5$\,pp (compressed) to $+4.6$\,pp (non-compressed; Appendix~\ref{app:fewnerd_epsilon}).

\subsection{Scaling and Inverse Scaling}\label{sec:scaling}

Oracle F1 follows $F_1(N) = a - b \cdot N^{-c}$ ($R^2 > 0.999$; Figure~\ref{fig:oracle_scaling}): Few-NERD ($c{\approx}0.61$) scales comparably to reasoning tasks \cite{brown2024monkeys}, SciERC converges more slowly ($c{\approx}0.35$), yet confidence-based aggregation recovers ${<}1$\,pp---a persistent gap.
The gap persists across scales and families: scaling from 8B to 14B FT increases oracle headroom ($+1.2$\,pp) with minimal greedy gain ($+0.9$\,pp), and GPT-5.5 (200 Few-NERD instances, zero-shot) exhibits the same pattern---50\% degeneracy, SJ $\rho{=}0.346$, MV $+1.4$\,pp yet 6.8\,pp oracle headroom unrealized.\footnote{Of the 10.1\% of GPT-5.5 samples producing empty entity sets, 88\% correspond to gold-empty instances; true parse failures affect only 1.2\% of samples (19/1{,}600) and shift all reported metrics by ${<}0.5$\,pp. See Appendix~\ref{app:frontier_sc}.}
Degeneracy is model-family-dependent rather than scale-dependent (Qwen2.5: $31.7$--$46.2$\% vs.\ Qwen3: $13.0$\% vs.\ GPT-5.5: $50$\% on Few-NERD; Appendix~\ref{app:cross_scale}).

\paragraph{Inverse scaling under adaptive thresholds.}
Increasing $N$ \textit{decreases} construction F1 in 40 of 58 transitions ($p{<}0.05$; Appendix~\ref{app:n_scaling}).
Methods using $\theta{=}2/N$ are most affected ($-3.09$\,pp at $N{=}8$, $-6.90$\,pp at $N{=}16$ vs.\ greedy on Few-NERD); majority vote ($\theta{=}\tfrac{1}{2}$) reduces the delta to $-0.87$/$-0.60$\,pp---severity reduction, not immunity (Table~\ref{tab:theta_sweep}).
Inverse scaling concentrates in non-degenerate instances ($11.1$\% vs.\ $1.3$\% for degenerate; OR${=}0.109$; Appendix~\ref{app:degen_inverse}).
Few-shot demonstrations improve QE (CoNLL SJ $\rho$ $.30{\to}.44$) but not construction (all n.s.; Appendix~\ref{app:fs_error}).

\subsection{Degeneracy Decomposition}\label{sec:theory}

\noindent\textbf{Degeneracy Decomposition.}\label{thm:degeneracy_bound}
For any aggregation method $A$: $\mathbb{E}[\Delta F_1(A)] \leq (1 - D) \cdot G_{\textup{nd}}$,
where $D$ is the degeneracy rate and $G_{\textup{nd}}$ the oracle gap on non-degenerate instances.
For signal-based methods with alignment $\alpha \in [0,1]$, this tightens to $(1{-}D) \cdot G_{\textup{nd}} \cdot \alpha$ (proof in Appendix~\ref{app:bound_proof}).

\noindent The bound is an intentionally loose \textit{necessary condition test}: when $D{\to}1$ or $\alpha{\to}0$, no aggregation method can improve over greedy, regardless of implementation.
It identifies \textit{where} aggregation fails---screening for favorable conditions---rather than quantitatively predicting gains.
Across 16 configurations, all gains respect the bound; the low recovery ratio (3--12\%; Figure~\ref{fig:bound}) reflects its role as a screening test, not a tight estimate.
$\alpha$---not $D$---is the binding constraint ($\alpha{=}0.000$--$0.161$; $8$--$33{\times}$ tighter), and this conclusion is robust to signal combination (\S\ref{sec:robustness_main}), verifier-based construction (\S\ref{sec:verifier}), and $\theta_{\text{crit}} \in [0.60, 0.80]$.

\paragraph{Bound looseness.}
The decomposition is a necessary condition screen showing how degeneracy and alignment jointly suppress gains, not a quantitative prediction tool. Two sources of looseness dominate: (1)~the entity independence assumption---split-half correlation $r{=}0.578$--$0.644$ reveals substantial inter-entity correlation structure within instances, which the bound ignores; (2)~$\alpha$ is estimated conservatively as the minimum across instances rather than an instance-adaptive value, further widening the gap. Together these explain the 3--12\% recovery ratio (bound ratio $0.13$--$0.63$). The decomposition nonetheless identifies $\alpha{\to}0$, not degeneracy, as the binding constraint across all tested configurations.

MV improves F1 only if marginal-entity precision exceeds $F_1^{\textup{gr}}/2$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:entity_selection_bound}; Appendix~\ref{app:alpha_crit}).
Table~\ref{tab:alpha_crit} validates: at $N{=}8$, no dataset meets this condition ($\Delta$ from $-2.74$ to ${\approx}0$\,pp); CoNLL ($\alpha_{\textup{crit,eff}}{=}1.148 {>} 1$) makes MV gain structurally impossible.

\section{Threshold Regime Analysis}\label{sec:theory_scaling}

\subsection{Entity Construction as MBR Decoding}\label{sec:mbr_theory}

Entity-level construction selects $\hat{y}_{\textup{MBR}} = \{e \in E_\cup : \hat{p}(e) > \alpha/(\alpha{+}1)\}$ under balanced set-overlap utility; $\alpha{=}1$ recovers majority vote (Proposition~\ref{prop:construction_mbr}; Table~\ref{tab:entity_construction}; Appendix~\ref{app:mbr_proof}).
Signal-derived weights $w_i$ yield quality-weighted MBR: $\hat{p}_w(e) = \sum_{i} w_i \, \mathbf{1}[e {\in} y_i] / \sum_{i} w_i$; weighting improves when $w_i$ correlates with instance quality but degrades otherwise (LP on SciERC: $\rho{\approx}0.2$; \S\ref{sec:prescriptive}), consistent with utility degradation on structured outputs \cite{eikema2025structured}.
We select $\varepsilon{=}0.05$ at the elbow of the compression curve, where LP-best selection advantage transitions from $+1.5$\,pp (compressed) to $+4.6$\,pp (non-compressed; Appendix~\ref{app:fewnerd_epsilon}).

\subsection{Scaling and Inverse Scaling}\label{sec:scaling}

Oracle F1 follows $F_1(N) = a - b \cdot N^{-c}$ ($R^2 > 0.999$; Figure~\ref{fig:oracle_scaling}): Few-NERD ($c{\approx}0.61$) scales comparably to reasoning tasks \cite{brown2024monkeys}, SciERC converges more slowly ($c{\approx}0.35$), yet confidence-based aggregation recovers ${<}1$\,pp---a persistent gap.
The gap persists across scales and families: scaling from 8B to 14B FT increases oracle headroom ($+1.2$\,pp) with minimal greedy gain ($+0.9$\,pp), and GPT-5.5 (200 Few-NERD instances, zero-shot) exhibits the same pattern---50\% degeneracy, SJ $\rho{=}0.346$, MV $+1.4$\,pp yet 6.8\,pp oracle headroom unrealized.\footnote{Of the 10.1\% of GPT-5.5 samples producing empty entity sets, 88\% correspond to gold-empty instances; true parse failures affect only 1.2\% of samples (19/1{,}600) and shift all reported metrics by ${<}0.5$\,pp. See Appendix~\ref{app:frontier_sc}.}
Degeneracy is model-family-dependent rather than scale-dependent (Qwen2.5: $31.7$--$46.2$\% vs.\ Qwen3: $13.0$\% vs.\ GPT-5.5: $50$\% on Few-NERD; Appendix~\ref{app:cross_scale}).

\paragraph{Inverse scaling under adaptive thresholds.}
Increasing $N$ \textit{decreases} construction F1 in 40 of 58 transitions ($p{<}0.05$; Appendix~\ref{app:n_scaling}).
Methods using $\theta{=}2/N$ are most affected ($-3.09$\,pp at $N{=}8$, $-6.90$\,pp at $N{=}16$ vs.\ greedy on Few-NERD); majority vote ($\theta{=}\tfrac{1}{2}$) reduces the delta to $-0.87$/$-0.60$\,pp---severity reduction, not immunity (Table~\ref{tab:theta_sweep}).
Inverse scaling concentrates in non-degenerate instances ($11.1$\% vs.\ $1.3$\% for degenerate; OR${=}0.109$; Appendix~\ref{app:degen_inverse}).
Few-shot demonstrations improve QE (CoNLL SJ $\rho$ $.30{\to}.44$) but not construction (all n.s.; Appendix~\ref{app:fs_error}).

\subsection{Degeneracy Decomposition}\label{sec:theory}

\noindent\textbf{Degeneracy Decomposition.}\label{thm:degeneracy_bound}
For any aggregation method $A$: $\mathbb{E}[\Delta F_1(A)] \leq (1 - D) \cdot G_{\textup{nd}}$,
where $D$ is the degeneracy rate and $G_{\textup{nd}}$ the oracle gap on non-degenerate instances.
For signal-based methods with alignment $\alpha \in [0,1]$, this tightens to $(1{-}D) \cdot G_{\textup{nd}} \cdot \alpha$ (proof in Appendix~\ref{app:bound_proof}).

\noindent The bound is an intentionally loose \textit{necessary condition test}: when $D{\to}1$ or $\alpha{\to}0$, no aggregation method can improve over greedy, regardless of implementation.
It identifies \textit{where} aggregation fails---screening for favorable conditions---rather than quantitatively predicting gains.
Across 16 configurations, all gains respect the bound; the low recovery ratio (3--12\%; Figure~\ref{fig:bound}) reflects its role as a screening test, not a tight estimate.
$\alpha$---not $D$---is the binding constraint ($\alpha{=}0.000$--$0.161$; $8$--$33{\times}$ tighter), and this conclusion is robust to signal combination (\S\ref{sec:robustness_main}), verifier-based construction (\S\ref{sec:verifier}), and $\theta_{\text{crit}} \in [0.60, 0.80]$.

\paragraph{Bound looseness.}
The decomposition is a necessary condition screen showing how degeneracy and alignment jointly suppress gains, not a quantitative prediction tool. Two sources of looseness dominate: (1)~the entity independence assumption---split-half correlation $r{=}0.578$--$0.644$ reveals substantial inter-entity correlation structure within instances, which the bound ignores; (2)~$\alpha$ is estimated conservatively as the minimum across instances rather than an instance-adaptive value, further widening the gap. Together these explain the 3--12\% recovery ratio (bound ratio $0.13$--$0.63$). The decomposition nonetheless identifies $\alpha{\to}0$, not degeneracy, as the binding constraint across all tested configurations.

MV improves F1 only if marginal-entity precision exceeds $F_1^{\textup{gr}}/2$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:entity_selection_bound}; Appendix~\ref{app:alpha_crit}).
Table~\ref{tab:alpha_crit} validates: at $N{=}8$, no dataset meets this condition ($\Delta$ from $-2.74$ to ${\approx}0$\,pp); CoNLL ($\alpha_{\textup{crit,eff}}{=}1.148 {>} 1$) makes MV gain structurally impossible.

# Response to Reviewers — R43

We thank both reviewers for their rigorous and constructive feedback. The central critique—that claims are stronger than evidence—is well-taken. We have performed a **systematic claim downgrade** throughout the paper: causal→correlational, prescriptive→exploratory, four-stage→three-stage contributions, and power-aware negative claims. Below we address each point with specific revisions.

---

## Must-Fix Responses

### MF1: Statistical Power — Negative Claims Need Power Qualification [R43-N1]
**Concern (R1 Must-Fix, R2 AGREE):** 2–3 seeds yield bootstrap CIs crossing zero (LP Δ 95% CI [−0.41, +2.54]). Cannot distinguish true null from insufficient power.

**Response:** Three changes address this:
1. **Limitations** now explicitly states: "Our negative selection claims are bounded by statistical power: with 2–3 seeds and MDE ≈1.5 pp, we cannot distinguish true null effects from small positive effects below detection threshold" (limitations.tex, line 6).
2. **§4** reports all selection gains with CI language: "LP achieves +0.2 pp (p=0.29), below MDE (≈1.5 pp at n=529, 2–3 seeds)" (single_signal.tex, line 39).
3. Throughout the paper, absolute negative claims ("fails", "no gain") are replaced with power-qualified language ("yields no detectable gains", "CI crosses zero").

**Paper location:** limitations.tex line 6, single_signal.tex lines 39–40, abstract.tex line 4.

---

### MF2: Bound Demoted from Independent Contribution [R43-N2]
**Concern (R1 Must-Fix, R2 AGREE):** §1 lists bound as one of four contributions, but §6.3 admits it's "intentionally loose." Framing inconsistency.

**Response:** The contribution structure is restructured from four stages to three:
1. **Discover** [§4]: QE signals achieve AUROC up to 0.82; instance-level decomposition reveals why correlation does not yield selection gains.
2. **Diagnose** [§4, §5, §6]: Diagnostic cascade—degeneracy, LP compression, signal alignment—quantifies failure mechanisms. The necessary condition bound (§6.3) is positioned *within* Diagnose as supporting analysis, not an independent contribution. Hidden-state probes reveal the introspection boundary (moved to Appendix reference).
3. **Construct (exploratory)** [§7.5]: Entity-level construction yields conditional gains under favorable diagnostic conditions.

The bound is no longer elevated as an independent contribution. §6.3 retains "intentionally loose necessary condition test" framing, now consistent with its role as a supporting diagnostic tool within the Diagnose stage.

**Paper location:** introduction.tex lines 23–31, §6.3 (theory.tex lines 27–29).

---

### MF3: Causal Language → Correlational/Observational [R43-N3]
**Concern (R1 Must-Fix, R2 strongly AGREE):** 11+ instances of causal language despite self-described observational design. §4 title implies causation.

**Response:** Systematic replacement across the paper (11 changes):
- **Abstract:** "jointly determine" → "are jointly associated with"
- **§1:** "jointly prevent selection" → "co-occur with selection failure"; added observational disclaimer: "our analysis is observational and all reported associations are correlational, not causal" (introduction.tex line 10)
- **§4 title:** "Where Single-Signal Selection Fails" → "Single-Signal Selection Results"
- **§4 body:** "effectively eliminating" → "leaving insufficient"
- **§6:** "localizes" → "identifies"
- **§8:** "localizing failure" → "identifying conditions associated with failure"; "eliminates...prevents" → "reduces...limits"
- **Discussion:** "prescriptive" → "preliminary check", "may warrant exploratory entity construction"

The paper now consistently uses correlational language throughout. The Few-NERD 3-vs-5 epoch comparison is explicitly framed as an observed association with a confound caveat, not a controlled experiment.

**Paper location:** abstract.tex line 5, introduction.tex line 10, single_signal.tex line 1 (title) and line 6, theory.tex, discussion.tex lines 8–9.

---

### MF4: Prescriptive → Exploratory [R43-N4]
**Concern (R2 Must-Fix, R1 AGREE):** Global Holm p_adj=0.055 is not significant. Per-family p_adj=0.006 relies on unregistered partition. Abstract places per-family before global, guiding attention to the more favorable number.

**Response:** Three changes:
1. **Contribution label:** "Prescriptive" → "Construct (exploratory)" in §1 (introduction.tex line 29).
2. **§7.5:** Opening paragraph and entity construction header now explicitly read "Entity-level construction (exploratory)" (experiments_main.tex line 104). Language changed from prescriptive recommendations to exploratory observations.
3. **Abstract p-value order swapped:** Now reads "global Holm p_adj=0.055, suggestive; per-family p_adj=0.006, post-hoc family partition" — global first, with explicit post-hoc annotation (abstract.tex line 6).

The paper no longer claims entity construction as a reliable prescriptive method. It is positioned as an exploratory finding under specific conditions, with transparent statistical caveats.

**Paper location:** abstract.tex line 6, introduction.tex line 29, experiments_main.tex lines 104, 109–110, discussion.tex line 9.

---

### MF5 (Divergent → Resolved): Title "Why" → "When" [R43-N5]
**Concern (R2 Must-Fix, R1 REBUT):** "Why SC Fails" is absolute; paper shows conditional success.

**Response:** Title changed to: **"When Self-Consistency Fails for NER: Degeneracy, Signal Collapse, and the Correlation-Selection Gap"** (main.tex line 28). "When" captures both the diagnostic (under what conditions does scaling fail?) and the conditional nature of findings (it sometimes succeeds).

---

## Should-Fix Responses

### SF1: Table 1 Dimension Overlap [R43-N6]
**Concern:** "Failure decomp." and "Diagnostics" overlap; Prescriptive row lacks p-value caveat.

**Response:** Table 1 reduced from 7 to 6 dimensions. "Failure decomp." and "Diagnostics" merged into a single "Diagnostic framework" row. "Prescriptive" row now reads "Conditional (p_adj=0.055)" to transparently signal statistical status.

**Paper location:** background.tex Table 1 (lines 24–34).

---

### SF2: Epoch Confound Baseline Difference [R43-W1]
**Concern:** 3-epoch model has lower greedy baseline; construction gains may partly reflect greater headroom.

**Response:** §7.5 now includes: "(note: 3-epoch greedy F1 0.748 vs 5-epoch 0.798; part of the larger Δ may reflect greater headroom under a weaker baseline)" (experiments_main.tex line 116). This explicitly flags the confound for readers.

---

### SF3: RE/SQL Abstract Reduction [R43-W2]
**Concern:** RE (n=397) and SQL (n=196) are too thin for "cross-task exploration."

**Response:** Abstract now reads "preliminary cross-task pilots (RE, SQL)" (abstract.tex line 3), further deemphasizing these extensions. Introduction frames them as "exploratory extensions" (line 14). No strong claims are made.

---

### SF4: Number Density [R43-W3]
**Concern:** Abstract has ~15 numerical values; §7 has 2–3 per sentence.

**Response:** Abstract numerical count reduced. Key numbers retained: AUROC 0.82, <1 pp selection gain, +1.40 pp entity construction, p-values (0.055, 0.006), 77–91% convergence collapse. Peripheral numbers (dataset counts, model sizes, seed counts) moved to Introduction or omitted from Abstract.

---

### SF5: Model Diversity [R43-W5]
**Concern:** Only Qwen + LLaMA; frontier degeneracy profiles differ substantially (5.5–74%).

**Response:** Limitations already states: "Frontier models exhibit markedly different degeneracy profiles (5.5–74%), suggesting findings from fine-tuned open-weight models may not fully generalize to proprietary systems" (limitations.tex line 1). This is an inherent scope limitation; we do not overclaim generalization.

---

### SF6: Practitioner Workflow [R43-W6]
**Concern:** §7.5 lacks concrete practitioner guidance.

**Response:** §7.5 now includes: "Practitioners can compute D and α on a pilot sample (N=8) to assess scaling viability before committing to repeated inference" (experiments_main.tex line 111). This provides actionable guidance: compute diagnostics cheaply before investing in full N-scaling.

---

### SF7: Missing References [R43-W8]
**Concern:** Malinin & Gales (2021) and Reflexion not discussed.

**Response:** Both added to §2 (Related Work):
- Malinin & Gales (2021) cited under "Uncertainty estimation and MBR" paragraph (background.tex line 16).
- Shinn et al. (2023, Reflexion) cited under "Test-time scaling and self-consistency" paragraph (background.tex line 5), with connection to our ESJ/MRSC negative results.

---

## Questions

### Q1: Bound Optimality
**Q:** Is the 3–12% recovery ratio optimal for this framework?

**A:** No. The bound is intentionally loose because diagnostic utility (screening) does not require quantitative precision. Two sources dominate looseness: (1) entity independence assumption (split-half r=0.578–0.644 reveals inter-entity correlation); (2) conservative α estimation as the instance minimum. Pursuing tighter bounds would require relaxing the independence assumption (entity-correlation-aware F1 decomposition), which we leave to future work. The key qualitative insight—α is 8–33× tighter than D—is robust regardless of bound tightness.

**Paper location:** §6.3 "Bound looseness" paragraph (theory.tex line 33).

---

### Q2: Free-Form RE Reversal
**Q:** LP selection reverses direction under free-form RE decoding. Is the gap decoding-strategy-dependent?

**A:** For NER, no: free-form ablation on SciERC, CoNLL, and Few-NERD shows LP std ratios of 0.97×, 0.86×, 1.00× respectively—LP compression is model-intrinsic. For RE, the reversal (+1.84±0.12 pp free-form vs −0.68 pp constrained) suggests the gap may be partially decoding-strategy-dependent in tasks where constrained decoding introduces format artifacts. This is task-specific and does not generalize to NER. Limitations notes the single-prompt-template scope.

**Paper location:** Appendix app:freeform_ablation, limitations.tex line 3.

---

### Q3: θ Selection Dependence
**Q:** θ∈[0.15, 0.35] across datasets—does this undermine pre-deployment diagnostics?

**A:** The θ sweep (Appendix app:theta_sweep) shows stable performance within this range; θ=2/N is a simple default that does not require held-out tuning. The practitioner diagnostic (compute D, α at N=8) assesses *whether* scaling is viable, not the optimal θ. If diagnostics indicate favorable conditions, θ=2/N is a reasonable starting point; grid search over θ would be a secondary optimization.

**Paper location:** experiments_main.tex line 105, Appendix app:theta_sweep.

---

### Q4: Degeneracy × Inverse Scaling Stratification
**Q:** Do high/low degeneracy subgroups show significantly different inverse scaling rates?

**A:** **Yes, strongly.** Post-hoc analysis across 4 datasets × N-transitions: degenerate instances show 1.3% inverse scaling rate vs non-degenerate instances 11.1% (OR=0.109, p<1e-300, Fisher's exact test). This is expected: degenerate instances produce identical entity sets across all N, so F1 is constant—they cannot exhibit inverse scaling by construction. Non-degenerate instances bear the full burden of threshold-sensitivity-driven inverse scaling. This directly supports the diagnostic framework: degeneracy partitioning identifies qualitatively different scaling regimes.

**Paper location:** Appendix app:degen_inverse (Table tab:degen_inverse), within §N-Scaling Detailed Analysis.

\section{Epoch Confound Analysis}\label{app:epoch_confound}

\paragraph{Training convergence modulates degeneracy.}
Table~\ref{tab:epoch_confound} compares the 3-epoch model (used throughout the main text) with a 5-epoch variant on Few-NERD (Qwen3-8B, $N{=}8$, $T{=}1.0$; full test set $n{=}32{,}565$, gold-filtered, 2-seed mean).
Extended training increases greedy F1 by $+0.7$~pp ($0.791 \to 0.798$) and triples instance degeneracy ($8.8$\% $\to$ $26.4$\%), reducing the fraction of instances with non-degenerate outputs.
The 5-epoch MV $\Delta$ ($-0.40$\,pp) appears smaller than 3-epoch ($-2.74$\,pp), but this is misleading: $26$\% of instances are fully degenerate (MV${\equiv}$greedy, $\Delta{=}0$), diluting the aggregate.
On non-degenerate instances, MV $\Delta{\approx}{-}0.55$\,pp, still negative---degeneracy masks the MV penalty rather than improving it.

LP selection shows even more dramatic degradation: 5-epoch LP $\Delta{=}{+}0.12{\pm}0.04$\,pp (2-seed, full test set micro-F1), a 91\% reduction from the 3-epoch $+1.39$\,pp. This confirms that training convergence not only increases degeneracy but also erodes LP's discriminative power within non-degenerate instances, consistent with the alignment degradation observed in SciERC (Table~\ref{tab:epoch_scierc}).

Evaluation loss increases after epoch 3, and the best checkpoint by validation loss occurs at approximately epoch 3.9.
Standard early stopping practice thus naturally selects the low-degeneracy regime.
This finding refines the narrative: degeneracy is not a fixed property of datasets but is modulated by the degree of training convergence. Over-trained models compress their output distributions, collapsing diversity even on datasets that support it under well-regularized training.

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\small
\caption{Training convergence confound on Few-NERD (Qwen3-8B, $N{=}8$, $T{=}1.0$, full test set $n{=}32{,}565$, gold-filtered, 2-seed mean). ``Degen.'': constant-F1 instance degeneracy. ``MV $\Delta$'': strict majority vote gain over greedy (pp). ``Non-degen MV $\Delta$'': MV gain on non-degenerate instances only.}
\label{tab:epoch_confound}
\resizebox{\columnwidth}{!}{
\begin{tabular}{lcc}
\toprule
Metric & 3-epoch & 5-epoch \\
\midrule
Greedy F1 & 0.791 & 0.798 \\
MV $\Delta$ (pp) & $-$2.74 & $-$0.40 \\
Instance degen.\ (\%) & 8.8 & 26.4 \\
SJ mean & 0.685 & 0.802 \\
LP $\Delta$ (pp) & $+$1.39 & $+$0.12${\pm}$0.04 \\
Entity constr.\ $\Delta$ (pp) & $+$0.88 & $+$0.20 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
}
\end{table}

\paragraph{SciERC epoch curve.}
Table~\ref{tab:epoch_scierc} extends the analysis to SciERC with a 3-point curve (3, 5, 10 epochs; Qwen3-8B, $N{=}8$, $T{=}1.0$).
Degeneracy increases monotonically (6.4\% $\to$ 17.8\% $\to$ 47.8\%), and within-instance LP-quality correlation degrades in tandem (median $\rho$: 0.319 $\to$ 0.262 $\to$ 0.112; mean $\rho$: 0.273 $\to$ 0.179 $\to$ 0.066), confirming that overtraining erodes both diversity and LP alignment simultaneously.
The fraction of instances with positive LP-quality correlation also declines (76.4\% at 3 epochs $\to$ 64.1\% at 5 epochs $\to$ 54.0\% at 10 epochs).
LP selection does not yield significant gains at any training duration ($-1.24$, $+0.64$, $+1.02$~pp; all below the ${\approx}$1.5~pp MDE), despite oracle headroom ranging from 8.4 to 15.0~pp.
The 3-epoch model has higher within-instance alignment ($\rho{=}0.319$) than the 5-epoch model ($\rho{=}0.262$), yet LP selection is worse ($-1.24$ vs.\ $+0.64$~pp): at 6.4\% degeneracy, more non-degenerate instances enter the candidate pool, but LP ranking precision is too low to exploit them, so the broader pool hurts rather than helps. This illustrates that low degeneracy does not ensure selection gains; LP-quality alignment predicts selection direction.
At 10 epochs, the model retains competitive greedy F1 (0.649 vs.\ 0.650 at 3 epochs) yet conditions are unfavorable: 47.8\% degenerate instances and $\rho{=}0.112$.
The gradient confirms that degeneracy is convergence-driven rather than a fixed dataset property: extended training compresses output distributions, degrading both diversity and within-instance alignment. However, the epoch-to-epoch alignment variation ($\Delta\rho_{\text{median}}{=}0.057$) is small relative to the cross-dataset gap (SciERC ${\sim}$0.3 vs.\ Few-NERD ${\sim}$0.5), consistent with alignment being primarily dataset-intrinsic: training convergence modulates alignment at the margin but cannot shift a dataset into the strong-alignment regime.
Even at the most favorable epoch (3-epoch, $\rho{=}0.319$), SciERC alignment remains below the ${\sim}$0.5 threshold associated with successful LP selection on Few-NERD.

\small
\caption{SciERC NER epoch curve (Qwen3-8B, $N{=}8$, $T{=}1.0$). Training duration modulates both instance degeneracy and within-instance LP-quality alignment. ``Degen.'': constant-F1 instance degeneracy (gold-filtered). ``LP $\Delta$'': LP selection gain over greedy (gold-filtered; none reaches the ${\approx}$1.5~pp MDE). ``$\rho$ med'': median within-instance LP-quality correlation. Greedy F1 uses span-based evaluation consistent with Tables 1--3; $\rho$ and LP $\Delta$ use text-based matching consistent with Table~\ref{tab:within_rho}.}
\label{tab:epoch_scierc}

\paragraph{TOST equivalence testing.}\label{app:tost}
The primary evidence against selection gains comes from effect sizes and confidence intervals: Cohen's $d{=}0.038$ for the best signal (NER LP) and bootstrap 95\% CI [$-$3.0, $+$4.2]~pp spanning zero.
Table~\ref{tab:tost} supplements this with two one-sided tests (TOST), testing whether each signal's selection F1 is equivalent to single-sample within a bound $\delta$.
The $\delta$ values are contextualized against oracle headroom (12--18~pp): $\delta{=}5$~pp corresponds to forgoing 28--38\% of the available headroom, $\delta{=}3$~pp forgoing 17--23\%, and $\delta{=}2$~pp less than 15\%.
These proportions use the same test data that defines the headroom, introducing circularity: $\delta$ is anchored to the very quantity it contextualizes.
We address this below with externally anchored equivalence margins.
The breakpoint $\delta^*$, the minimum equivalence margin at which each signal passes TOST, ranges from approximately 1.3~pp (SJ, ${\sim}$10\% of oracle headroom) to 3.4~pp (FK, ${\sim}$26\%) on NER, and from approximately 2.9~pp (LP, ${\sim}$16\%) to 6.5~pp (VC, ${\sim}$36\%) on RE.
On NER ($n{=}529$), at $\delta{=}{\pm}2$~pp, SJ and LP are confirmed equivalent to single-sample (TOST $p{<}0.05$); at $\delta{=}{\pm}3$~pp, four of five signals pass; at $\delta{=}{\pm}5$~pp, all five pass.
On RE ($n{=}397$, preliminary), EM and VC fail equivalence even at $\delta{=}{\pm}5$~pp due to systematic underperformance ($\Delta{=}{-}3.2$~pp and $-4.5$~pp respectively).
The effect sizes are negligible ($d{=}0.038$) and confidence intervals span zero, with TOST confirming equivalence at practically meaningful margins.

1	\section{Threshold Regime Analysis}\label{sec:theory_scaling}
2	
3	\subsection{Entity Construction as MBR Decoding}\label{sec:mbr_theory}
4	
5	Entity-level construction selects $\hat{y}_{\textup{MBR}} = \{e \in E_\cup : \hat{p}(e) > \alpha/(\alpha{+}1)\}$ under balanced set-overlap utility; $\alpha{=}1$ recovers majority vote (Proposition~\ref{prop:construction_mbr}; Table~\ref{tab:entity_construction}; Appendix~\ref{app:mbr_proof}).
6	Signal-derived weights $w_i$ yield quality-weighted MBR: $\hat{p}_w(e) = \sum_{i} w_i \, \mathbf{1}[e {\in} y_i] / \sum_{i} w_i$; weighting improves when $w_i$ correlates with instance quality but degrades otherwise (LP on SciERC: $\rho{\approx}0.2$; \S\ref{sec:prescriptive}), consistent with utility degradation on structured outputs \cite{eikema2025structured}.
7	We select $\varepsilon{=}0.05$ at the elbow of the compression curve, where LP-best selection advantage transitions from $+1.5$\,pp (compressed) to $+4.6$\,pp (non-compressed; Appendix~\ref{app:fewnerd_epsilon}).
8	
9	\subsection{Scaling and Inverse Scaling}\label{sec:scaling}
10	
11	Oracle F1 follows $F_1(N) = a - b \cdot N^{-c}$ ($R^2 > 0.999$; Figure~\ref{fig:oracle_scaling}): Few-NERD ($c{\approx}0.61$) scales comparably to reasoning tasks \cite{brown2024monkeys}, SciERC converges more slowly ($c{\approx}0.35$), yet confidence-based aggregation recovers ${<}1$\,pp---a persistent gap.
12	The gap persists across scales and families: scaling from 8B to 14B FT increases oracle headroom ($+1.2$\,pp) with minimal greedy gain ($+0.9$\,pp), and GPT-5.5 (200 Few-NERD instances, zero-shot) exhibits the same pattern---50\% degeneracy, SJ $\rho{=}0.346$, MV $+1.4$\,pp yet 6.8\,pp oracle headroom unrealized.\footnote{Of the 10.1\% of GPT-5.5 samples producing empty entity sets, 88\% correspond to gold-empty instances; true parse failures affect only 1.2\% of samples (19/1{,}600) and shift all reported metrics by ${<}0.5$\,pp. See Appendix~\ref{app:frontier_sc}.}
13	Degeneracy is model-family-dependent rather than scale-dependent (Qwen2.5: $31.7$--$46.2$\% vs.\ Qwen3: $13.0$\% vs.\ GPT-5.5: $50$\% on Few-NERD; Appendix~\ref{app:cross_scale}).
14	
15	\paragraph{Inverse scaling under adaptive thresholds.}
16	Increasing $N$ \textit{decreases} construction F1 in 40 of 58 transitions ($p{<}0.05$; Appendix~\ref{app:n_scaling}).
17	Methods using $\theta{=}2/N$ are most affected ($-3.09$\,pp at $N{=}8$, $-6.90$\,pp at $N{=}16$ vs.\ greedy on Few-NERD); majority vote ($\theta{=}\tfrac{1}{2}$) reduces the delta to $-0.87$/$-0.60$\,pp---severity reduction, not immunity (Table~\ref{tab:theta_sweep}).
18	Inverse scaling concentrates in non-degenerate instances ($11.1$\% vs.\ $1.3$\% for degenerate; OR${=}0.109$; Appendix~\ref{app:degen_inverse}).
19	Few-shot demonstrations improve QE (CoNLL SJ $\rho$ $.30{\to}.44$) but not construction (all n.s.; Appendix~\ref{app:fs_error}).
20	
21	\subsection{Degeneracy Decomposition}\label{sec:theory}
22	
23	\noindent\textbf{Degeneracy Decomposition.}\label{thm:degeneracy_bound}
24	For any aggregation method $A$: $\mathbb{E}[\Delta F_1(A)] \leq (1 - D) \cdot G_{\textup{nd}}$,
25	where $D$ is the degeneracy rate and $G_{\textup{nd}}$ the oracle gap on non-degenerate instances.
26	For signal-based methods with alignment $\alpha \in [0,1]$, this tightens to $(1{-}D) \cdot G_{\textup{nd}} \cdot \alpha$ (proof in Appendix~\ref{app:bound_proof}).
27	
28	\noindent The bound is an intentionally loose \textit{necessary condition test}: when $D{\to}1$ or $\alpha{\to}0$, no aggregation method can improve over greedy, regardless of implementation.
29	It identifies \textit{where} aggregation fails---screening for favorable conditions---rather than quantitatively predicting gains.
30	Across 16 configurations, all gains respect the bound; the low recovery ratio (3--12\%; Figure~\ref{fig:bound}) reflects its role as a screening test, not a tight estimate.
31	$\alpha$---not $D$---is the binding constraint ($\alpha{=}0.000$--$0.161$; $8$--$33{\times}$ tighter), and this conclusion is robust to signal combination (\S\ref{sec:robustness_main}), verifier-based construction (\S\ref{sec:verifier}), and $\theta_{\text{crit}} \in [0.60, 0.80]$.
32	
33	\paragraph{Bound looseness.}
34	The decomposition is a necessary condition screen showing how degeneracy and alignment jointly suppress gains, not a quantitative prediction tool. Two sources of looseness dominate: (1)~the entity independence assumption---split-half correlation $r{=}0.395$--$0.578$ (Table~\ref{tab:fk_independence}) reveals substantial inter-entity correlation structure within instances, which the bound ignores; (2)~$\alpha$ is estimated conservatively as the minimum across instances rather than an instance-adaptive value, further widening the gap. Together these explain the 3--12\% recovery ratio (bound ratio $0.13$--$0.63$). The decomposition nonetheless identifies $\alpha{\to}0$, not degeneracy, as the binding constraint across all tested configurations.
35	
36	MV improves F1 only if marginal-entity precision exceeds $F_1^{\textup{gr}}/2$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:entity_selection_bound}; Appendix~\ref{app:alpha_crit}).
37	Table~\ref{tab:alpha_crit} validates: at $N{=}8$, no dataset meets this condition ($\Delta$ from $-2.74$ to ${\approx}0$\,pp); CoNLL ($\alpha_{\textup{crit,eff}}{=}1.148 {>} 1$) makes MV gain structurally impossible.

We select $\varepsilon{=}0.05$ at the elbow of the compression curve, where LP-best selection advantage transitions from $+1.5$\,pp (compressed) to $+4.6$\,pp (non-compressed; Appendix~\ref{app:fewnerd_epsilon}).

\subsection{Scaling and Inverse Scaling}\label{sec:scaling}

Oracle F1 follows $F_1(N) = a - b \cdot N^{-c}$ ($R^2 > 0.999$; Figure~\ref{fig:oracle_scaling}): Few-NERD ($c{\approx}0.61$) scales comparably to reasoning tasks \cite{brown2024monkeys}, SciERC converges more slowly ($c{\approx}0.35$), yet confidence-based aggregation recovers ${<}1$\,pp---a persistent gap.
The gap persists across scales and families: scaling from 8B to 14B FT increases oracle headroom ($+1.2$\,pp) with minimal greedy gain ($+0.9$\,pp), and GPT-5.5 (200 Few-NERD instances, zero-shot) exhibits the same pattern---50\% degeneracy, SJ $\rho{=}0.346$, MV $+1.4$\,pp yet 6.8\,pp oracle headroom unrealized.\footnote{Of the 10.1\% of GPT-5.5 samples producing empty entity sets, 88\% correspond to gold-empty instances; true parse failures affect only 1.2\% of samples (19/1{,}600) and shift all reported metrics by ${<}0.5$\,pp. See Appendix~\ref{app:frontier_sc}.}
Degeneracy is model-family-dependent rather than scale-dependent (Qwen2.5: $31.7$--$46.2$\% vs.\ Qwen3: $13.0$\% vs.\ GPT-5.5: $50$\% on Few-NERD; Appendix~\ref{app:cross_scale}).

\paragraph{Inverse scaling under adaptive thresholds.}
Increasing $N$ \textit{decreases} construction F1 in 40 of 58 transitions ($p{<}0.05$; Appendix~\ref{app:n_scaling}).
Methods using $\theta{=}2/N$ are most affected ($-3.09$\,pp at $N{=}8$, $-6.90$\,pp at $N{=}16$ vs.\ greedy on Few-NERD); majority vote ($\theta{=}\tfrac{1}{2}$) reduces the delta to $-0.87$/$-0.60$\,pp---severity reduction, not immunity (Table~\ref{tab:theta_sweep}).
Inverse scaling concentrates in non-degenerate instances ($11.1$\% vs.\ $1.3$\% for degenerate; OR${=}0.109$; Appendix~\ref{app:degen_inverse}).
Few-shot demonstrations improve QE (CoNLL SJ $\rho$ $.30{\to}.44$) but not construction (all n.s.; Appendix~\ref{app:fs_error}).

\subsection{Degeneracy Decomposition}\label{sec:theory}

\noindent\textbf{Degeneracy Decomposition.}\label{thm:degeneracy_bound}
For any aggregation method $A$: $\mathbb{E}[\Delta F_1(A)] \leq (1 - D) \cdot G_{\textup{nd}}$,
where $D$ is the degeneracy rate and $G_{\textup{nd}}$ the oracle gap on non-degenerate instances.
For signal-based methods with alignment $\alpha \in [0,1]$, this tightens to $(1{-}D) \cdot G_{\textup{nd}} \cdot \alpha$ (proof in Appendix~\ref{app:bound_proof}).

\noindent The bound is an intentionally loose \textit{necessary condition test}: when $D{\to}1$ or $\alpha{\to}0$, no aggregation method can improve over greedy, regardless of implementation.
It identifies \textit{where} aggregation fails---screening for favorable conditions---rather than quantitatively predicting gains.
Across 16 configurations, all gains respect the bound; the low recovery ratio (3--12\%; Figure~\ref{fig:bound}) reflects its role as a screening test, not a tight estimate.
$\alpha$---not $D$---is the binding constraint ($\alpha{=}0.000$--$0.161$; $8$--$33{\times}$ tighter), and this conclusion is robust to signal combination (\S\ref{sec:robustness_main}), verifier-based construction (\S\ref{sec:verifier}), and $\theta_{\text{crit}} \in [0.60, 0.80]$.

\paragraph{Bound looseness.}
The decomposition is a necessary condition screen showing how degeneracy and alignment jointly suppress gains, not a quantitative prediction tool. Two sources of looseness dominate: (1)~the entity independence assumption---split-half correlation $r{=}0.395$--$0.578$ (Table~\ref{tab:fk_independence}) reveals substantial inter-entity correlation structure within instances, which the bound ignores; (2)~$\alpha$ is estimated conservatively as the minimum across instances rather than an instance-adaptive value, further widening the gap. Together these explain the 3--12\% recovery ratio (bound ratio $0.13$--$0.63$). The decomposition nonetheless identifies $\alpha{\to}0$, not degeneracy, as the binding constraint across all tested configurations.

MV improves F1 only if marginal-entity precision exceeds $F_1^{\textup{gr}}/2$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:entity_selection_bound}; Appendix~\ref{app:alpha_crit}).
Table~\ref{tab:alpha_crit} validates: at $N{=}8$, no dataset meets this condition ($\Delta$ from $-2.74$ to ${\approx}0$\,pp); CoNLL ($\alpha_{\textup{crit,eff}}{=}1.148 {>} 1$) makes MV gain structurally impossible.

\section{Epoch Confound Analysis}\label{app:epoch_confound}

\paragraph{Training convergence modulates degeneracy.}
Table~\ref{tab:epoch_confound} compares the 3-epoch model (used throughout the main text) with a 5-epoch variant on Few-NERD (Qwen3-8B, $N{=}8$, $T{=}1.0$; full test set $n{=}32{,}565$, gold-filtered, 2-seed mean).
Extended training increases greedy F1 by $+0.7$~pp ($0.791 \to 0.798$) and triples instance degeneracy ($8.8$\% $\to$ $26.4$\%), reducing the fraction of instances with non-degenerate outputs.
The 5-epoch MV $\Delta$ ($-0.40$\,pp) appears smaller than 3-epoch ($-2.74$\,pp), but this is misleading: $26$\% of instances are fully degenerate (MV${\equiv}$greedy, $\Delta{=}0$), diluting the aggregate.
On non-degenerate instances, MV $\Delta{\approx}{-}0.55$\,pp, still negative---degeneracy masks the MV penalty rather than improving it.

LP selection shows even more dramatic degradation: 5-epoch LP $\Delta{=}{+}0.12{\pm}0.04$\,pp (2-seed mean), a 91\% reduction from the 3-epoch $+1.39$\,pp (both evaluated on the full test set under identical conditions; Table~\ref{tab:epoch_confound}). This confirms that training convergence not only increases degeneracy but also erodes LP's discriminative power within non-degenerate instances, consistent with the alignment degradation observed in SciERC (Table~\ref{tab:epoch_scierc}).

Evaluation loss increases after epoch 3, and the best checkpoint by validation loss occurs at approximately epoch 3.9.
Standard early stopping practice thus naturally selects the low-degeneracy regime.
This finding refines the narrative: degeneracy is not a fixed property of datasets but is modulated by the degree of training convergence. Over-trained models compress their output distributions, collapsing diversity even on datasets that support it under well-regularized training.

\small
